$CNX | @crynuxio might be one of the more overlooked projects in the decentralized AI sector.

55 million tasks completed during testnet.

1,785 participating nodes.

A working AI chat and image-generation application.

And 71% of $CNX supply allocated to task mining tied to network usage.

Here’s why I’ve been paying attention 🔽

1️⃣ Turning idle GPUs into productive infrastructure

There are millions of GPUs sitting inside gaming PCs and other computers around the world.

Many of them remain underutilized for significant portions of the day.

Crynux is building a decentralized network that allows GPU owners to contribute their computing resources to AI workloads.

Instead of relying entirely on centralized infrastructure providers, developers can access computational power supplied by independent operators.

The arrangement is straightforward:

→ GPU owners contribute computing power.

→ Developers use that power to run AI applications.

→ Operators earn $CNX for completing tasks.

The interesting part is that a computer in one part of the world can process an AI request originating from an application thousands of kilometres away.

And the network handles the coordination.

2️⃣ But does decentralized AI actually work?

This was the question I wanted answered.

A decentralized computing network sounds promising in theory, but the real test is whether it can deliver something people can actually use.

That’s where Crynux Chat comes in.

It’s a working AI application powered by the Crynux network, with a free demo that anyone can explore.

You can interact with AI models, ask questions, generate content, and even create images.

For example, one of the demonstrations involves generating an image of a small red lighthouse on a snowy cliff at dusk.

Here’s what happens behind the scenes.

When you submit the prompt:

→ Crynux-AS submits the task to the network.

→ The blockchain assigns an available GPU node.

→ The node receives the task through a relay and runs the AI model.

→ The network performs the required validation.

→ The generated image returns to your chat.

And you can actually follow the progress.

The interface shows the different stages: In Queue, Generating, Verifying, Uploading, and Finishing.

The example uses Qwen Image 2.1, with the actual computation performed by a GPU node participating in the network.

It’s a simple demonstration, but it makes the underlying technology much easier to understand.

3️⃣ Solving the trust problem

Now comes one of the more interesting technical challenges.

If anyone can contribute hardware, how does the network know that operators are completing tasks correctly?

After all, decentralized infrastructure can’t simply assume every participant is honest.

Crynux addresses this through its verification system, vssML.

Rather than duplicating every computation, the network uses unpredictable checks.

Approximately 10% of tasks are selected for independent verification, with results compared across three nodes.

Operators don’t know beforehand which tasks will be checked.

And because they have $CNX at stake, submitting dishonest results carries financial consequences.

The objective is to make dishonest behaviour economically unattractive while avoiding the enormous cost of independently repeating every computation.

4️⃣ More than just AI chatbots

Crynux Chat is one application built on the network, but the potential use cases extend considerably further.

The infrastructure supports workloads involving:

→ AI chatbots and virtual assistants

→ Text generation, translation, and summarization

→ Code generation and debugging

→ AI image generation and editing

→ Model fine-tuning

→ LoRA training and customization

For developers, another important feature is compatibility with familiar AI development tools and request formats.

That means existing applications can potentially integrate Crynux without rebuilding their entire AI infrastructure.

And this is important because the easier it becomes for developers to access decentralized computing, the easier it becomes for the network to attract real workloads.

5️⃣ The $CNX economics are particularly interesting

This is one aspect I think deserves more attention.

71% of the maximum $CNX supply is allocated to task mining.

But unlike conventional token emission schedules, these allocations are linked to network demand and completed work.

In other words, the task-mining allocation isn’t simply released because another month has passed.

Actual network activity drives its distribution.

Why does this matter?

Because many crypto projects experience supply expansion regardless of whether their products attract meaningful adoption.

Crynux takes a different approach with its task-mining allocation.

Of course, this doesn’t eliminate dilution altogether. Other token allocations and circulating supply dynamics still matter.

But linking a substantial portion of token distribution to actual computational work creates an interesting relationship between network usage and token issuance.

It’s a model worth watching as adoption develops.

6️⃣ Where does Crynux stand today?

Crynux launched its mainnet in June 2026.

Before that, its testnet recorded:

→ 1,785 participating nodes

→ 55 million completed tasks

Those figures provide some early evidence of network activity, although sustained mainnet usage will ultimately be the more important measure.

There’s also a fairly accessible way for newcomers to explore the ecosystem.

Crynux Chat offers a free demo with a limited daily allowance.

Users can try AI conversations and image generation without immediately needing to purchase tokens.

Wallet connectivity is optional for users who want to access their own Crynux credits.

One important detail: conversations are stored locally in the browser, and GPU node operators may have access to the information necessary to process requests. Sensitive information should therefore never be submitted.

✦ My perspective

I’ve always been more interested in crypto projects that build technology people have a practical reason to use.

And decentralized AI computing is an area I believe deserves serious attention.

The demand for AI computation is real. The hardware needed to supply it already exists.

The opportunity lies in connecting those resources efficiently, making the computation reliable, and building an ecosystem that developers actually want to use.

That’s the opportunity Crynux is pursuing.

The next questions are whether the network can attract sustained developer demand, remain cost-competitive, and scale reliably.

Those are the metrics I’ll be paying attention to.

For now, @crynuxio is firmly on my radar.

And $CNX is one I’ll be watching closely.

Higgsfield reached a $5.4 BILLION valuation while most AI video companies are still fighting over who has the best model.

they started with AI video creation. then cinematic tools, AI influencers, marketing studios, and now they're letting people create mobile games from a single prompt.

every new angle gives them access to an entirely different customer.

a filmmaker, an ecommerce brand, and a mobile game publisher can all discover Higgsfield for completely different reasons.

that's the strategy worth copying.

here's how i'd replicate their playbook for FREE

1. Steal the market research, not the product.

find 5 competitors already getting millions of views.

go through their most popular posts, ads, and Reddit discussions. look for repeated complaints, unanswered questions, or things people wish existed.

for example, if people keep complaining that mobile game ads look more fun than the games themselves, that's an opportunity to build a playable version of a similar concept.

you're using research your competitors already spent money gathering.

2. Hijack attention that's already there.

instead of trying to make an AI influencer famous from zero, attach the character to something people already care about.

say a mobile game ad goes viral.

have your AI streamer try to beat the challenge, criticize the game design, or show a better version.

make comparison videos targeting the exact game people are searching for.

you're borrowing existing demand instead of trying to create it yourself.

3. Sell the same thing from five different angles.

one AI character could be:

a gaming influencer promoting app installs
a streamer doing sponsored challenges
a character appearing inside playable ads
a virtual host reviewing new AI tools
a mascot that smaller brands can license

same character. different audience. different reason to pay.

you don't need five businesses to test five markets.

4. Turn complaints into content.

find a competitor's most controversial feature.

read 50 comments and identify what people actually dislike.

make your next video about that exact problem.

if people hate misleading game ads, have your influencer show the difference between the advertisement and the real gameplay.

controversy gets attention, but solving the complaint gives people a reason to follow you.

5. Treat tiny changes like new launches.

Higgsfield constantly introduces new ways to use its products.

do the same thing with your content.

change the character's role, the opening sentence, the audience, or the offer.

one week she's a streamer challenging viewers to beat her score. the next she's reviewing mobile game ads. then she's hosting a sponsored competition.

announce each new format, measure the response, and keep the ones that attract buyers.

6. Build distribution without paying for ads.

find 20 small creators whose audiences already match the product.

offer them a custom AI video or playable challenge they can post, with a revenue share on any sales they generate.

they get new content without paying upfront. you get access to an audience you haven't built yet.

repeat with different niches until you find one that converts.

the bigger lesson here is that Higgsfield doesn't wait until its original market is saturated before exploring another one.

it keeps giving new groups of people a reason to use its technology.

and that's what i'd copy.

most people spend months trying to perfect one AI influencer.

i'd rather test 20 different reasons someone might want to watch, share, or pay for that same character.

you only need one of those angles to open up an entirely new market....

Opera wants websites to run AI on your laptop instead of sending your data to the cloud | Paulo Vargas, Digital Trends

Opera wants to move routine AI work out of distant data centers and onto the computer already sitting on your desk. Its new WebAI preview lets websites and browser extensions use local models inside Opera One without requiring another AI subscription or sending the information they handle to a cloud service.

WebAI also opens local AI to third-party developers instead of reserving it for Opera’s own features. Your laptop supplies the computing power, provided it has enough to spare.

How WebAI puts models to work

WebAI is a proposed web standard that gives websites and extensions access to AI through the browser. Opera says the effort has backing from Google and Microsoft. Its implementation is model-agnostic and centered on open models.

Opera One can tap Google’s Gemma models, while compatible Macs can also use Apple’s on-device foundation model. Developers can generate or classify text without maintaining their own AI servers or paying for every request sent to an outside service.

Opera’s examples are deliberately practical and a little nosy. One extension can sort a messy tab collection, while another can flag clickbait before it eats another five minutes of your life.

What stays under your control

Opera has kept WebAI disabled by default. Nothing is downloaded until the user enables it, and each site needs permission before it can access the browser’s local AI. That extra layer is important when websites, rather than only Opera, can call the models running on your computer.

No data center will rescue weaker hardware, however. Speed and capability depend on the computer, and Opera hasn’t disclosed minimum performance requirements beyond the supported platforms. Opera GX and Opera Neon are scheduled to receive WebAI later.

Why Opera also built a bulldozer

Opera is pairing WebAI with a separate experiment called HTML-in-Canvas. It lets developers place functional webpages inside 2D and 3D scenes, where buttons and forms keep working as the page moves through virtual space.

The showcase includes a Gamer Room with live webpages on its screens and Webpage Bulldozer, which turns site elements into objects you can shove around. Both demos already work in Opera browsers without setup, so the bulldozer is the part anyone can try while WebAI remains an opt-in early preview.

The whole world is turning into a casino

I keep seeing the same mistake. Crypto bros, tech bros, now AI bros too, notice some insanity in their own industry and assume it’s unique to crypto, AI or tech.

It isn’t.

Crypto is just an exaggerated version of the rest of the world.

In crypto, leverage, memecoins and pure gambling are everywhere.

But the same mechanics are leaking into normal life too.

- Open a marketplace app: spin the wheel.
- Open a supermarket app: scratch a card.
- McDonald’s runs Monopoly with instant prizes. Instacart tested a literal virtual wheel of fortune.

random reward → jackpot → try again → maybe you’ll get lucky

And actual gambling is growing too.

- According to Pew Research, 31% of Americans under 30 bet on sports in the previous year.

The share betting online went from 7% in 2022 to 17% in 2025.

And no, this isn’t just an American thing.

- According to Russian bookmaker market research cited by Vedomosti, 13 million Russians placed at least one bet in 2025, while the number of active bettors rose 9.4% to 6.9 million.

The share of people who see betting as a regular source of extra income also rose from 15.3% to 19.1%.

Americans and Russians: brothers forever.

For young people, gambling is starting to look like one of the few ways to radically change your life.

Housing is expensive. Career paths feel less reliable. Dating is a mess. Nobody knows what AI will replace next.

The casino at least offers one simple promise:

WHAT IF I GET LUCKY AND GET RICH?

And technology makes the whole thing frictionless.

Phone in your pocket. A few clicks. Spin a wheel. Place a bet. Open 100x leverage.

Yes, conspiracy guys: Squid Game was the warm-up.

If this keeps going, you end up with a huge number of people who don’t see a clear future, but do have anger, desperation and a taste for risk.

Where does that energy go?

More gambling? Radical politics? Emigration? Apathy? Some new historical disaster?

No idea.

But if we get really unlucky:

Should a diffusion model in online RL be the policy, or the thing that proposes plans?

GTP (Generative Trajectory Planning; Harvard, NeurIPS 2026) argues for the second. Like TD-MPC2, it plans through learned dynamics, reward and value models, but the candidate action sequences come from a diffusion prior instead of Gaussian sampling.

Beam search refines the candidates by partially re-noising and denoising them, and the best plans are distilled back into the prior, so search and proposals improve each other. When acting, the agent plans optimistically across a dynamics ensemble; when building value targets, it plans conservatively.

• Locomotion: highest mean return on all five Gym MuJoCo tasks after 1M steps, e.g. Humanoid 6,660 vs 5,269 for the best baseline; on Ant it is level with TD-MPC2

• Manipulation: on PushT from pixels it reaches 99% after 1M steps, while TD-MPC2 needs 3M steps to reach 97% and SAC and DreamerV3 stay at 0%

• Cost: action selection is on par with TD-MPC2 (34 vs 36 ms on an RTX 5090), but a training update takes 157 ms vs 4 ms, or 19 ms when planned trajectories are reused

• Deployment: the trained prior alone, without any search, keeps 99% success on FetchPickAndPlace at 8.6 ms per action
